First of all, I am totally ignorant about categorifying things in Lean. It looks so heavy that I would not like to touch it unless necessary in my first project. Unfortunately, I encountered it when writing down the following definition IsAdmissible(I omit the open-compact condition here for simplicity)

variable {G : Type*} [Group G]
variable {k : Type*} [Field k]
variable {V : Type*} [AddCommGroup V] [Module k V]

def IsAdmissible (ρ : Representation k G V) : Prop :=
    ∀ (K : Subgroup G),
    FiniteDimensional k (invariants (Rep.res K.subtype (Rep.of ρ)).ρ)

In mathlib, the restriction of scalar functor between representations categories along monoids morphism is only defined at the category level, namely the Rep.res, while most part of Mathlib.RepresentationTheory is written at the object level, e.g. invariants has domain Representation k G V not Rep k G. Therefore, I have to switch between Rep and Representation using Rep.of and .ρ in the above definition.

Why do we choose to have Rep.res defined at the categorical level while let others be defined at the object level? For kind of definitions/results should I postpone until the categorical language has been developed? Or should I just give an expanded definition here to avoid combining invariants and Rep.res awkwardly?

One of the reasons why we want to use category theory a lot when studying representations is that their cohomology is often crucial and this is better done in the category theory library that encompasses homological algebra. So i would suggest to work in Rep as much as possible rather than in Representation.

OK, I will try. Have you ever considered some systematical LLM process here? Upgrading things from the object level to the categorical level seems nasty in Lean but often mathematically boring (please let me know if this is not the case)
I find it great fun, but it's personal taste. In particular, I've personally never tried writing serious lean with an LLM.

@Filippo A. E. Nuccio my recommendation would be just the opposite -- work in Representation as much as possible and then deduce things for Rep. Why? (1) Beginner project (2) no universe issues (3) we don't normally take cohomology of smooth admissible representations, the big goals are things like local Langlands which is just about the irreducible representations (4) local Langlands can be "categorified" nowadays but the right object isn't just the category of all smooth representations, it's some derived category of solid ell-adic sheaves on Bun_G. So I am not sure I see any need for the category you're proposing.

@Kevin Buzzard , I see your points, and you're perhaps right. But I know @Jiaxi Mo personally (he followed my classes in Beijing) and I'm sure 1+2 are not a problem. 3) is a good point and I was a bit too much focused on answering the question "why do we have so much category theory in Mathlib to speak about representation"? rather than on smooth ones. For 4), I'm less sure: precisely because we want to probably work in a derived category, developing the API directly for, at least, chain complexes rather than simple objects seems easier. But at the end, as usual, it will most be during the production of the API that we'll realize what the best approach is, I believe. At any rate, of course, you're the Langlands expert :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

I think that right now in representation theory we want to develop both the category and the non category approach and my instinct here would be "develop the non category approach and then deduce the category version" but this is only because of historical memories of pain going the other way, which after the recent changes might no longer be relevant. If you start with a Representation and then make a Rep and then the Representation again (eg you're developing the theory using Representation and then jump to Rep just to do one thing and then jump back again) then a while ago you would run into the problem that the new V was defeq to the old V but not syntactically equal, so typeclass inference would synthesize a new group action which was only defeq to the original one after unfolding. This really hurt people like Amelia, although with the recent changes I no longer know how painful this is. But this is my real reason for worrying a bit when I see "doesn't exist in Representation so pop into Rep to do it". My instinct is that the required construction (eg invariants in this case) would be better off made in Representation rather than going into category land and back. But as I say my worries might be to a certain extent out of date.

I believe the correct way to define the category of smooth representations is to define it as the full subcategory of Rep consisting of smooth representations. Proving SmoothRep is an abelian category could be reduced to proving Rep is abelian and ker coker of morphisms between smooth representations (and then reduced to sub/quot) are smooth. The latter is easy and is on object level. Therefore, even if, by any chance, you wish to have a nice smooth representation category to do cohomological algebra, there is no need to develop things from the begining. But based on my understanding,Rep has not been developed to its final stable form yet, and I am not sure how long it will take for the reviewers to digest such a categorifying programm (afterall Rep.basic has 1000+ lines, and for me, is much less readable than Representation).
Note that we have, or we will soon have, continuous representations, so you may want to follow the same path. cc @Edison Xie
And I am also developing unitary representations in MeanFourier

@Riccardo Brasca Yeah, I noticed that file. But I guess the theory will diverge from continuous very soon: it is rather easy to define internal Hom and tensor productin the smooth case, which will be used in the discussion of cuspidality (something again much more tailored for the smooth theory). That's one of my motivation to build up seperate file for smooth representations
Oh yes, I absolutely agree we want a new file!

I actually have the same suggestion as Kevin, we should stay in the concrete world as much as possible. And in terms of restriction I think this actually showed one problem I explained to @Riccardo Brasca , so right now the restriction in Representation is just literally compose the representation with a monoid homomorphism which is bad (we definitely should not abuse defeq like this) because right now Representation is an abbrev of monoid homomorphism! I think at some point we (probly me) should refactor it into an one field structure of the monoid homomorphism!

@Edison Xie Thanks for your comment! For the moment, the best choice might be the following :

def IsAdmissible (ρ : Representation k G V) : Prop :=
    ∀ (K : OpenCompactSubgroup G),
    FiniteDimensional k (invariants (MonoidHom.comp ρ K.subtype))
Did you write the definition of OpenCompactSubgroup? I couldn't find it anywheree

Sorry, I forgot that I have removed it for simplicity at the begining of this post. The answer is: yes, but locally on my PC

structure OpenCompactSubgroup (G : Type*) [TopologicalSpace G] [Group G] [IsTopologicalGroup G]
    extends Subgroup G where
  isOpen' : IsOpen (toSubgroup : Set G)
  isCompact' : IsCompact (toSubgroup : Set G)

Since there were different suggestions among experts about categorifying things, I decided to try it myself (The progess can be checked now in #41199 Representation.Smooth.SmRep, which complies and includes the instance of a closed braided monoidal stucture at the moment). The fun part is that the nasty naturality condition can almost be solved by cat_disch! One exception is the naturality of tensorHomEquiv, which was eventually solved by Adjunction.restrictFullSubcategory. At the end, the compatiblity of dualizing functor and the contragredient is proved by rfl. This is crazy! Now I agree that it is great fun @Filippo A. E. Nuccio. The painful part is the abelian category structure, which can be done in an ad hoc way, but the I couldn't locate the desired API in Rep (e.g. mono corresponds to subrepresentation)
